what: Normal shipping will not resume in strait of Hormuz until 80 mines cleared

clean_source_blocks.text: Tanker owner trade body says centre of strait will remain closed for ‘some time’, with vessels risking running aground by taking Omani route The centre of the strait of Hormuz is blocked with about 80 mines that will need clearing for normal shipping to resume, the independent tanker owner trade body has said. Several vessels began to exit the Gulf through the key maritime chokepoint on Thursday, after the signing of a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran. Continue reading...

Tanker owner trade body says centre of strait will remain closed for ‘some time’, with vessels risking running aground by taking Omani route The centre of the strait of Hormuz is blocked with about 80 mines that will need clearing for normal shipping to resume, the independent tanker owner trade body has said. Several vessels began to exit the Gulf through the key maritime chokepoint on Thursday, after the signing of a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran. However, shipping is not expected to return to normal for some time, even if the ceasefire lasts, because of the mines and other obstacles, underlining the continuing challenges facing global trade. “The main route … through the middle of the strait of Hormuz, that’s closed, that’s dangerous,” said Phil Belcher, marine director at Intertanko, the association of independent tanker owners.

“The latest figure we had was that there’s 80 mines in the strait of Hormuz. It’s an enormous amount and it’s going to take some time to clear.” During the conflict Tehran laid mines in the centre of the strait in the traffic separation scheme, which has been in place between Iran and Oman since 1968, to restrict the movement of tankers and other vessels. About 20,000 seafarers were left stuck either side of the channel, although some ships managed to sneak through at night near the Omani coast with their transmitters off and with US assistance. Others paid to travel through Iranian waters in an arrangement nicknamed “Tehran’s tollbooth”.

The shipping industry is keen to see a return to using the standard route, which before the conflict allowed about 130 ships a day to safely cross the strait, through which about 20% of global oil used to flow. “This is like a highway where the road in the middle is closed and you are using the hard shoulder,” said Belcher. “We need to get the highway open so we can get the volume of traffic through safely. One of the big issues we’ve got at the moment is the navigational risk, the risk of running aground on the rocks. It’s very close to the rocks on the southern route, the Omani route.”

payload.title: Hormuzinsalmen normaali laivaliikenne odottaa miinojen raivausta
payload.summary: Hormuzinsalmen keskiväylä pysyy suljettuna arviolta noin 80 miinan vuoksi, eikä normaali meriliikenne ole palaamassa heti, vaikka Yhdysvaltojen ja Iranin yhteisymmärrys on avannut reittiä osalle aluksista.
payload.content:
Hormuzinsalmen normaali laivaliikenne ei ole palaamassa vielä ennalleen, koska salmen keskiosassa on riippumattomien tankkerinomistajien etujärjestön mukaan noin 80 miinaa. Osa aluksista alkoi torstaina poistua Persianlahdelta Yhdysvaltojen ja Iranin allekirjoittaman yhteisymmärryspöytäkirjan jälkeen, mutta merenkulun pääreittiä pidetään yhä vaarallisena.

## Keskiväylä on edelleen suljettu

Intertankon meriasioista vastaavan johtajan Phil Belcherin mukaan Hormuzinsalmen keskellä kulkeva pääreitti on suljettu ja vaarallinen. Hänen mukaansa viimeisin arvio kertoo noin 80 miinasta, joiden raivaaminen vie aikaa.

Miinat asetettiin konfliktin aikana salmen keskiosan liikenteenjakovyöhykkeelle. Kyseinen järjestely on ollut Iranin ja Omanin välillä käytössä vuodesta 1968, ja sen tarkoituksena on ohjata tankkereiden ja muiden alusten kulkua turvallisesti kapean merialueen läpi.

## Kiertoreitti lisää merenkulun riskejä

Vaikka osa aluksista on päässyt liikkeelle, varustamot eivät pidä tilannetta normaalina. Belcher vertasi tilannetta tiehen, jonka keskikaistat ovat poissa käytöstä ja liikenne joutuu käyttämään pientareen kaltaista reittiä.

Eteläisempi Omania sivuava reitti on käytössä, mutta siihen liittyy navigointiriski. Alukset kulkevat lähellä karikkoisia alueita, mikä lisää pohjakosketuksen vaaraa. Jo konfliktin aikana osa laivoista kulki öisin Omanin rannikon tuntumassa lähettimet suljettuina ja Yhdysvaltojen avustuksella. Osa puolestaan maksoi kulusta Iranin vesien kautta.

## Salmen merkitys korostaa raivauksen kiirettä

Hormuzinsalmi on maailmankaupan kannalta keskeinen merireitti. Ennen konfliktia sen kautta kulki noin 130 alusta päivässä, ja salmen kautta virtasi noin viidennes maailman öljystä. Merenkulkuala haluaa palata tavanomaiselle reitille juuri siksi, että suuri liikennemäärä voidaan hoitaa turvallisemmin vakiintuneella väylällä kuin kapealla eteläisellä kiertoreitillä.

Tilanne on jättänyt noin 20 000 merenkulkijaa odottamaan salmen eri puolille. Vaikka tulitauko pitäisi, miinat ja muut esteet merkitsevät, että normaalin liikenteen palautuminen riippuu ennen kaikkea pääväylän turvallisesta raivaamisesta.

Osa aluksista on alkanut poistua Persianlahdelta Yhdysvaltojen ja Iranin sopimuksen jälkeen.
Omanin rannikon läheinen kiertoreitti lisää pohjakosketuksen riskiä.

Tanker owner trade body says centre of strait will remain closed for ‘some time’, with vessels risking running aground by taking Omani route The centre of the strait of Hormuz is blocked with about 80 mines that will need clearing for normal shipping to resume, the independent tanker owner trade body has said. Several vessels began to exit the Gulf through the key maritime chokepoint on Thursday, after the signing of a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran. However, shipping is not expected to return to normal for some time, even if the ceasefire lasts, because of the mines and other obstacles, underlining the continuing challenges facing global trade. “The main route … through the middle of the strait of Hormuz, that’s closed, that’s dangerous,” said Phil Belcher, marine director at Intertanko, the association of independent tanker owners.

“The latest figure we had was that there’s 80 mines in the strait of Hormuz. It’s an enormous amount and it’s going to take some time to clear.” During the conflict Tehran laid mines in the centre of the strait in the traffic separation scheme, which has been in place between Iran and Oman since 1968, to restrict the movement of tankers and other vessels. About 20,000 seafarers were left stuck either side of the channel, although some ships managed to sneak through at night near the Omani coast with their transmitters off and with US assistance. Others paid to travel through Iranian waters in an arrangement nicknamed “Tehran’s tollbooth”.

The shipping industry is keen to see a return to using the standard route, which before the conflict allowed about 130 ships a day to safely cross the strait, through which about 20% of global oil used to flow. “This is like a highway where the road in the middle is closed and you are using the hard shoulder,” said Belcher. “We need to get the highway open so we can get the volume of traffic through safely. One of the big issues we’ve got at the moment is the navigational risk, the risk of running aground on the rocks. It’s very close to the rocks on the southern route, the Omani route.”
